His 93.0 mph average exit velocity sits at the 95th percentile, his xwOBA is .379, and a 13.0% walk rate next to an 18.2% strikeout rate describes a hitter who punishes pitchers for missing the zone rather than one who simply swings hard at everything. If the bat stays where Statcast says it belongs, he's a perennial middle-of-the-order fixture before his 25th birthday.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The Statcast contact profile is almost comically lopsided: a 22.1% barrel rate and 95.2 mph average exit velocity that both sit at the 100th percentile, yet a 31.2% whiff rate that lands at the 16th. He makes brutal, legitimate contact when he finds the ball, and he draws walks at a 16.9% clip that keeps the on-base number honest even when the swings and misses pile up. The whole profile hinges on whether pitchers can live in that whiff zone long enough to neutralize the .425 xwOBA, because if they can, the 29.4% strikeout rate becomes a real drag on a 745-PA season. If it holds together the way the quality-of-contact metrics suggest it can, you're looking at a 40-homer, .912 OPS outfielder at 23, which is a straightforward star.

Against that contact quality, a 29.9% whiff rate reads less as a flaw and more as the price of hunting elite velocity, because his 14.3% walk rate confirms the zone management is sound where it matters. On the mound, a 2.72 xERA and a 30.4% whiff rate describe a genuine frontline starter, not a curiosity, with a 98.1 mph fastball doing real work. The whole profile hinges on health, specifically whether he holds a full DH workload while returning to a starter's innings count, and if that holds, the projection line of .280/.389/.538 with 38 home runs is the floor, not the ceiling.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xwOBA and the walk rate are pointing in the same direction: something real is happening here. Crow-Armstrong's .361 xwOBA sits in the 86th percentile, his 11.8% walk rate is well above the league norm, and his 47.5% hard-hit rate does the work of explaining why the contact quality holds up even with a 25.9% strikeout rate that looks a little ugly on the surface. The chase rate, at 34.9%, is the thing to watch — that's a 20th-percentile figure, and if pitchers keep expanding him successfully the walk rate compresses and the whole contact profile gets harder to trust. If it holds, the projection's .854 OPS with 31 home runs and 38 stolen bags is a legitimate outcome for a 24-year-old whose speed grades at 29.5 ft/s, 96th percentile, and who already knows how to take a pitch.

reports.name: Elly De La Cruz
reports.published_report: The contact profile is genuinely strange for someone hitting the ball this hard. De La Cruz's 94.2 mph average exit velocity sits at the 99th percentile, and his 15.0% barrel rate and 52.2% hard-hit rate produce an xSLG of .491 and an xwOBA of .367 that match almost exactly what the projection asks of him: .838 OPS, 28 home runs, 30 steals across 631 plate appearances. The problem is the 27.1% strikeout rate, which bleeds into everything and is the only thing keeping this from being a top-ten conversation. If he trims the swing-and-miss, the raw power and sprint speed (.271/.347/.491 with 30 bags is the floor, not the ceiling) make him one of the more terrifying offensive profiles in the sport; if he doesn't, you're living with a genuinely elite slugger who leaves too many walks on the table to reach his ceiling.

reports.published_report: The tension in this profile is extreme and it's right there in the contact numbers: an 18.4% walk rate sitting alongside a 36.8% whiff rate, both near the outer edges of what the majors see. Kurtz generates 93.6 mph average exit velocity with an 18.1% barrel rate, which is why the .379 xwOBA reads as legitimate despite a .250 xBA — he destroys what he makes contact with, but he swings through a lot of pitches first. The whole profile hinges on whether pitchers can force him into more two-strike counts and shrink that walk rate, because a 31.6% strikeout rate is already a significant tax on the production. If the contact rates hold where they are, the projection's .898 OPS with 31 home runs is a fair accounting of what he produces; if pitchers learn to attack him within the zone and his 22.8% chase rate creeps up, the strikeouts compound and the walks evaporate, and you're left with raw power trapped inside a very lossy profile.

reports.name: Cam Schlittler
reports.published_report: A 2.68 ERA projection over 186.6 innings with a 1.04 WHIP is a number worth stopping on, and the Statcast profile explains why it's believable. His 5.1% walk rate sits in the 95th percentile, and a 34.9% chase rate tells you hitters are expanding the zone against him, so the 29.7% strikeout rate is being built on location and deception as much as raw stuff, even though 97.8 mph with elite fastball spin gives him plenty of both. The one friction point is the barrel rate, a middling 8.3%, which means when hitters do make contact, the damage isn't as suppressed as the xwOBA and xERA suggest, and that gap between a 3.03 xERA and a 2.68 projection hinges on sequencing and strand rates holding through a full rotation load. If it does, he's a genuine top-of-rotation arm; if the barrels cluster at the wrong moments, the ERA drifts toward the xERA and you have a very good number-two.

reports.name: Jacob Wilson

Wilson's 11.1% strikeout rate sits in the 96th percentile, and his 14.3% whiff rate is similarly elite, but his average exit velocity of 83.8 mph is at the 1st percentile, meaning he makes extraordinary contact with very ordinary authority. reports.name: Nelson Rada
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 385 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact and walk rates are genuinely exciting; the power is the problem. Rada is hitting .286/.389 at AAA with 50 walks against just 59 strikeouts in 385 plate appearances, and the translation says that discipline holds up at the big-league level: an 18.4% strikeout rate that would play comfortably, and a 10.8% walk rate that clears the 8.5% MLB average by a meaningful margin. But 2 home runs in those same 385 plate appearances says the bat is essentially all contact and speed, and a translated ISO of .093 against a .150 MLB average tells you the gap doesn't close when the level goes up. The 29 stolen bases give the profile something real to lean on, and if a plus-contact center fielder with that kind of on-base ability can carve out a role without power, there's a bench or platoon piece here; if the power never arrives, what's left is a very good organizational asset running out of ceiling.

reports.name: Chandler Simpson
reports.published_report: One homer projected across 559 plate appearances, and that's not the weird part. The weird part is that it might not matter. Simpson makes contact at a 9.3% strikeout rate that sits at the 99th percentile, and his 29.5 ft/s sprint speed makes every ball in play a problem for the defense, which is how a .288 projected average survives a .294 xSLG and 14.4% hard-hit rate that both bottom out at the 1st percentile. The whole profile hinges on whether that contact quality is survivable at scale, because his xwOBA of .264 leaves almost no margin for regression in the batting average — the speed and the bat-to-ball are doing every bit of the offensive work, and 40 projected steals tell you exactly what kind of player he is when the bat quiets down. A low-end regular or a very fast bench piece, depending entirely on whether a .325 OBP holds in a full season against pitchers who learn to throw him strikes.

reports.name: TJ Rumfield

reports.name: Sam Antonacci
reports.published_report: The contact grades are the story here, and they don't match the rest of the profile. The problem is that 87.5 mph average exit velocity and a 36.2% hard-hit rate sit near the bottom of the league in raw power, so the xSLG of .426 is getting built almost entirely on placement and contact shape rather than authority. The projection's .275/.366/.403 line holds together if he stays this disciplined and keeps finding gaps, but a 7.4% walk rate means the plate approach is less patient than it looks — he's earning his .366 OBP by making contact, not drawing free passes, and any drift in bat-to-ball quality collapses the profile fast. This reads as a legitimate second-division regular, maybe an everyday player if the hit tool keeps translating; without the contact grades, there's a 21-steal, no-power outfielder with a middling OBP and not much else.

reports.name: Michael King
reports.published_report:
The Statcast card and the projection are telling very different stories, and understanding which one to believe is the whole argument.

Current-season Statcast has him at a 4.62 xERA with a 9.7% walk rate and only 20.7% strikeouts, a contact-suppression profile that doesn't hold water when hitters are barreling him at 8.6% and making hard contact at 33.2%. The projection bets on 3.52 ERA over 186.2 innings, leaning on that 87.3 mph average exit velocity as evidence the hard contact hasn't actually hurt him yet. If the walk rate stays near double digits and the strikeout rate doesn't climb, you're looking at a back-end starter who runs out of margin; if the contact quality stays as suppressed as the exit velocity suggests, he's a legitimate mid-rotation piece who earns those 16 quality starts.

reports.name: Caden Bodine
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with medium risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 152 A PA.
reports.published_report: The contact profile is almost impossible to believe for a 22-year-old catcher: just 20 strikeouts across 373 plate appearances at AA & A+ & A, a 5 K% that translates to 12.1% against big-league pitching while the MLB average sits at 22.0%. The .356/.426/.528 line across those levels is built on genuine bat-to-ball rather than a BABIP mirage, with a .350 BABIP grounding a .172 ISO that has some real pop behind it. The ceiling question is power: the MLB-equivalent ISO translates to .124, short of the 8.5% walk rate that separates a platoon bat from an everyday catcher, and if the gap between his raw pop and its MLB translation holds, the upside is a bench piece who earns a roster spot on contact alone. Bodine either develops enough thump to push into a regular role, or he becomes one of those rare bench catchers who almost never strikes out and quietly sticks for a decade.

reports.name: Shota Imanaga
reports.published_report: A 36.8% chase rate is the whole argument. That figure sits at the 96th percentile, meaning hitters are chasing Imanaga's stuff at a rate almost no starter in baseball can match, and it explains how a 91.8 mph fastball still generates a 29.3% whiff rate without elite strikeout numbers to show for it — the 23.5% K rate is essentially average, but he's manufacturing weak contact and empty swings through location and deception rather than pure stuff. The 6.0% walk rate, at the 85th percentile, keeps him from needing to attack the zone out of desperation, which is exactly the pitcher who sustains a 3.75 xERA over a full rotation slot. The barrel rate at 9.9% is the one soft spot in the profile, sitting at just the 18th percentile, so if his command slips and he catches more of the zone, the contact quality could drift in a bad direction; the projection at a 3.94 ERA over 180.5 innings assumes that doesn't happen often enough to matter.

reports.name: Ryan O'Hearn
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is solidly average, and that's actually the tension. His 45.5% hard-hit rate is a genuine loud number, well above the middle of the pack, but a 7.8% barrel rate keeps the damage from concentrating, and the xSLG of .419 trails the projected .448 SLG, meaning the full-season projection carries some optimism on the slug side. At 32, with a 7.9% walk rate that sits below average and a chase rate in the bottom third of the league, the profile hinges on whether he continues to put enough of that hard contact in good spots to sustain real run production. If he does, a .271/.337/.448 line over 579 plate appearances is a perfectly useful first baseman, just not one who wins you a position.

Depth arm, ceiling and floor both.

reports.name: Jim Jarvis
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 348 AAA PA.
reports.published_report:

reports.name: Jake Bennett
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.98 and the walk rate at 4.4%, and those two numbers are basically the whole argument for Bennett. He doesn't miss many bats, with an 18.7% strikeout rate and a 23.4% whiff rate both below average, but a 37.3% chase rate and soft contact allowed at 86.8 mph average exit velo mean hitters are beating themselves when they expand. The fastball at 92.9 mph with 2155 rpm spin won't overpower anyone, so the profile hinges on whether that chase-driven approach holds up against lineups seeing him repeatedly. If it does, the projection's 3.37 ERA across 113.7 innings looks conservative; if big-league hitters start laying off, there isn't a swing-and-miss floor to catch him.

reports.name: Hayden Alvarez
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 399 A PA.
reports.published_report: The stolen base total is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the most honest thing about it. Forty-one steals across 399 plate appearances at A ball, with a .402 OBP to get on base and a 14% walk rate to stay there, is a real skill set — Alvarez can create runs without waiting for the ball to leave the yard. The trouble is that the MLB-equivalent translation knocks the ISO down to .121, which is a gap ball hitter's number, and the strikeout rate inflates to 26.3%, which leaves a profile that, if the speed translates and nothing else grows, is a bench piece rather than a center-field regular. He's 19, which is the only thing that keeps the ceiling language from closing entirely, but the floor here is bench or depth, and that feels honest given where the power and contact are headed at the next level.

reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.name: Jacob Melton
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 139 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The .391 BABIP is the first thing to squint at, and it's also the first thing that could make this whole read moot. Across 139 AAA plate appearances, Jacob Melton is hitting .272/.377/.500 with 20 stolen bases, and the numbers that survive a BABIP correction are the ones worth watching: 20 walks against 44 strikeouts, with an ISO that translates to .163 in MLB context against a league where the average sits at .15. That strikeout rate translates to 27%, well above the 22% MLB baseline, and at a contact floor that shaky, the ISO needs to hold to keep the profile interesting. If the BABIP normalizes and the strikeouts stay, what's left is a bench outfielder with some speed and fringe power, not nothing, but not a regular.

reports.name: Tsung-Che Cheng
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 240 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the honest edge here. Thirty-two walks in 240 AAA plate appearances translates to a 10.5% walk rate against an MLB average of 8.5%, which is a real skill and the thing that keeps his profile from being merely a glove-and-speed placeholder. The speed is loud too, 10 stolen bases already this season, and the .351 OBP at AAA reflects both. Where it gets complicated is the power: a .17 ISO at AAA softens to .142 in MLB equivalent terms, right at or just below league average, which means the offensive profile leans heavily on getting on base rather than doing damage once he does. If the walk rate travels and the contact holds, 60 strikeouts in 240 PA is a tick above comfortable at the big-league level, Cheng is a viable bench bat who can play shortstop and run; if the strikeout rate creeps and the ISO doesn't grow, the floor is organizational depth.

reports.name: Tekoah Roby
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with high risk. The current pitching shape is mixed over 47 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The control is what makes this profile worth a second look. Across 47 innings at AA, Roby posted a 2.1 BB/9 and a 1.0 WHIP, and when that command translates to an MLB context across AAA & AA, the walk rate holds — 2.7 BB/9, comfortably better than the MLB average, with a K-BB% that lands at 15.1%. The strikeout rate is the asterisk: his K/9 translates to 8.5, essentially matching what an average MLB arm produces, which means the profile lives or dies on whether the command stays elite enough to compensate. If it does, he's a useful depth piece who earns a rotation spot in a pinch; if the stuff doesn't miss enough bats against better competition, he settles into a bullpen role where the control still plays.
